lessons.title: Study Session 1: Working Out the True Cost of a Unit or Service

blocks.text: Introduction Achol Deng bakes and sells bread from a small stall in Yei, and had always worked out what a loaf cost her by adding up flour and sugar alone, until a slow month forced her to look closer and she found that once firewood, her own time at the oven and the stall's rent were counted in, several of her loaves had been selling for barely more than they cost to make. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about how small enterprises actually set their selling prices. Distinguish a cost built from materials alone from a true, full cost per unit. Apply a method for building a full cost per unit from materials, labour and overhead. Recognise the risk of pricing a product from an incomplete cost figure. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Loaf That Cost More Than the Flour Achol Deng's bread stall in Yei had, since its very first day of trading, priced a loaf by adding together the cost of flour and sugar and stopping there. During a slow month, Achol sat down to work out why the stall was struggling despite steady sales, and began listing every cost the bread actually carried: firewood for the oven, the hours she spent baking each morning, and a share of the small rent she paid for the stall. Once those were added in, several of her loaves proved to be selling for barely more than they cost to produce. 2.2 What Research Found About How SMEs Set Their Prices Pambo Bigambo, Salum Marandu and Elias Elias studied twenty metalwork small and medium enterprises in Dar es Salaam for a 2023 paper, examining how these businesses actually arrived at a selling price for what they made. Many of the enterprises studied set prices using only direct material cost, leaving out labour and overhead almost entirely, a pattern the researchers linked to selling prices that failed to reflect the full cost of production. 2.3 Building a Full Cost Per Unit Listing Every Cost a Unit Actually Carries Setting down, on paper, every cost that goes into producing one unit, materials, the time spent making it, and a fair share of costs like rent or fuel that are not tied to any single unit, gives a far more complete figure than materials alone ever can. Dividing Shared Costs Across the Units That Cause Them Taking a shared cost such as rent or firewood and spreading it evenly across the number of units typically produced in that period turns an overhead expense that feels abstract into a concrete amount that belongs on each unit. 2.4 Key Practices List every cost a unit carries, not only its materials. Assign a fair share of rent, fuel or other shared costs to each unit produced. Include the value of your own labour time, even where no wage is formally paid. Recalculate the full cost whenever a material or shared cost changes noticeably. 2.5 A Worked Example: Achol's Full Cost Per Loaf Achol worked out that a single loaf used roughly the equivalent of two hundred South Sudanese pounds in flour and sugar, but that firewood added a further sixty, her own baking time added another ninety once valued fairly, and a share of the stall's weekly rent added forty more. The full cost of one loaf came to almost double what Achol's material-only figure had shown, and several of her prices sat only just above that true figure. With the full cost in front of her, Achol adjusted the prices on her lowest-margin loaves and left her already well-priced items untouched, and the following month's earnings reflected the change clearly. Achol's original habit of costing from flour and sugar alone had not been an attempt to cut corners. Costs that were real but easy to overlook had simply gone uncounted, and only listing every one of them ever showed what a loaf genuinely cost to bring to the counter. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Costing a product from its materials alone, without including labour or a share of overhead, makes it impossible to tell whether a price actually covers what the product costs to make, exactly what happened with Achol's loaves. Treating one's own working time as free, rather than assigning it a fair value, quietly understates the true cost of almost anything a small enterprise produces. 2.7 Materials Are Only Part of What a Unit Costs Achol's flour and sugar figures had never once been wrong in themselves. Accuracy in that narrow figure had never meant it captured the whole cost of a loaf, and only counting firewood, time and rent alongside it ever showed what bread at that stall genuinely cost to make. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build a full cost per unit from materials, labour and a fair share of overhead. Study Session 2 turns from knowing a unit's true cost to deciding deliberately how much to add on top of it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about a product or service you offer. Does its price reflect materials alone, or a full cost including your time and shared expenses? 2. Work out the full cost per unit for one real product or service, listing materials, labour and a fair share of overhead. Practical Output: Practical Output A full cost-per-unit worksheet for one real product or service, listing materials, labour and a fair share of overhead separately before totalling them. 7.0 References and Further Reading Bigambo, P., Marandu, S., & Elias, E. (2023). Product costing and pricing in small and medium enterprises in Tanzania. Tanzania Journal of Engineering and Technology, 42(2), 141 to 157. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 27:26, on lambs being for clothing and goats the price of a field. Qur'an, Surah Al-Hijr 15:19, on the earth spread out and caused to grow every kind of thing in due proportion.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Setting a Margin on Top of True Cost

blocks.text: Introduction Hodan Robleh spends her evenings looking after her father, whose health has been failing for some years, and fills her days embroidering dresses to sell from home in Ali Sabieh, and had always set a price by guessing at what felt fair, until comparing her guessed prices against a properly calculated margin showed that some of her most detailed dresses were badly underpriced while a few simpler ones were priced well above what a reasonable margin would suggest. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about pricing strategy and SME growth. Distinguish a deliberately set margin from a guessed price. Apply a method for adding a margin to a true cost figure. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Price Set by Feel, Not by Figures Hodan Robleh's embroidery business in Ali Sabieh had always priced each dress by a kind of instinct, a number that felt roughly fair given the work involved, without ever calculating a true cost or a deliberate margin on top of it. When Hodan finally worked out the true cost of several dresses and compared it against her usual asking prices, she found that her most heavily embroidered pieces, the ones that took the longest, were priced with almost no margin at all, while a few simpler dresses carried a margin far larger than she had realised. 2.2 What Research Found About Pricing Strategy and SME Growth Nothemba Hope Ndwandwe and Floyd Khoza surveyed 132 small and medium enterprises operating in a South African municipality for a 2026 study, examining how deliberate pricing strategy related to business growth and sustainability. A significant and positive relationship was found between having a deliberate pricing strategy and both the growth and the sustainability of the enterprises studied, distinguishing businesses that priced with intent from those that did not. 2.3 Adding a Deliberate Margin to True Cost Choosing a Margin Before Setting Any Price Deciding on a margin, whether a fixed percentage or a fixed amount, before working out any individual price keeps that margin consistent from one item to the next, instead of shifting on instinct each time. Applying the Same Margin Consistently Across Similar Items Using the same chosen margin on every item within a similar category, rather than adjusting it case by case based on how a price feels, keeps pricing fair to the business and predictable for the person setting it. 2.4 Key Practices Choose a margin, whether a percentage or a fixed amount, before pricing any individual item. Apply the chosen margin consistently across items in a similar category. Compare a guessed price against the margin-based price before finalising it. Revisit the chosen margin periodically rather than assuming it still fits. 2.5 A Worked Example: Hodan's Consistent Margin Hodan chose a fixed margin of forty percent above true cost for every dress, regardless of how simple or detailed the embroidery, and reworked her price list against that rule rather than against how each price felt. Her most heavily embroidered dresses rose in price noticeably, while a couple of simpler dresses actually came down, and customers accepted both changes without complaint once Hodan could explain what each price reflected. Within two months, Hodan's income from dress sales had grown even though the number of dresses she sold stayed roughly the same, since her prices now consistently reflected the work behind each piece. Nothing careless had sat behind Hodan's earlier guessed prices. They had simply been set without a deliberate margin to anchor them, and only choosing one and applying it consistently ever brought her prices in line with the effort each dress actually required. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Setting a price by instinct, without first calculating true cost or choosing a deliberate margin, leaves a business vulnerable to underpricing its most demanding work, exactly what happened with Hodan's most detailed dresses. Applying a different margin to similar items depending on how a price feels in the moment removes the predictability that a chosen, consistent margin is meant to provide. 2.7 A Fair-Feeling Price Is Not the Same as a Calculated One Hodan's guessed prices had genuinely felt reasonable to her at the time she set each one. Feeling reasonable had never guaranteed that a price actually reflected the cost and effort behind it, and only comparing her guesses against a deliberately chosen margin ever revealed where those two things had quietly pulled apart. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to add a deliberate margin on top of a true cost figure rather than guessing at a price. Study Session 3 turns from setting an individual price to working out the minimum volume a business needs to sell before it turns a profit at all.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about how you currently set prices. Do they come from a deliberate margin, or from a sense of what feels fair? 2. Choose a margin and apply it consistently to reprice three real items, comparing the result against your previous guessed prices. Practical Output: Practical Output A repriced list of at least three real items using one consistently applied margin, compared against the previous guessed prices for each. 7.0 References and Further Reading Ndwandwe, N.H., & Khoza, F. (2026). The impact of pricing strategies on the growth and sustainability of small and medium enterprises: Empirical evidence from South Africa. Businesses, 6(1), Article 10. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 31:16, on considering a field and buying it, planting a vineyard with the fruit of her hands. Qur'an, Surah An-Nahl 16:14, on ships ploughing through the sea that you may seek of His bounty.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Finding the Break-Even Point

blocks.text: Introduction Ilda Fortes processes and bottles fruit juice out of her home in Assomada, and had run the business for two years without ever working out how many bottles she needed to sell each month just to cover her costs, until a slow month left her unable to tell whether it was a genuine loss or simply normal variation, and a proper break-even calculation finally gave her a real number to measure against. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about break-even analysis among micro, small and medium enterprises. Distinguish a break-even volume from an arbitrary sales target. Apply a method for calculating a break-even point. Recognise what a break-even point does and does not tell a business. Apply break-even thinking to a specific change in cost or price. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Slow Month With No Number to Measure Against Ilda Fortes had run her fruit juice bottling business in Assomada for two years without ever calculating how many bottles she needed to sell in a month simply to cover her costs. When a particularly slow month arrived, Ilda had no way to tell whether the business had genuinely lost money or whether the slowdown sat within normal variation, since she had never worked out the one number that would have told her where that line actually sat. 2.2 What Research Found About Break-Even Analysis Among MSMEs Lucia Sintha examined the use of break-even analysis among micro, small and medium enterprises for a 2020 study, noting that a substantial share of the businesses that stop trading do so partly because they never carried out a profit and loss or break-even calculation. Applying a break-even model was found to be straightforward even for enterprises with simple bookkeeping, and owners who applied it reported a clearer understanding of their own cost structure afterward. 2.3 Calculating a Break-Even Point Separating Fixed Costs From the Margin Each Unit Earns Adding up the costs that stay the same regardless of how much is sold, then dividing that total by the margin each unit earns above its own variable cost, gives the exact number of units that must be sold before those fixed costs are covered. Treating the Break-Even Number as a Floor, Not a Target Using the break-even figure as the minimum a business must clear, rather than as a goal to aim for, keeps the focus on staying safely above it instead of merely reaching it. 2.4 Key Practices Separate fixed costs from the margin each unit earns above its variable cost. Divide total fixed costs by the margin per unit to find the break-even volume. Recalculate break-even whenever a fixed cost or a price changes. Track actual sales against the break-even figure each month, not only at the end of the year. 2.5 A Worked Example: Ilda's Break-Even Bottle Count Ilda totalled her fixed monthly costs, kitchen rent, a fruit press lease and a fixed transport fee, and found they came to just over twenty-two thousand escudos. Each bottle of juice earned a margin of roughly two hundred escudos above its own ingredients and packaging, which meant Ilda needed to sell around one hundred and ten bottles a month before any profit began. With that figure in hand, Ilda could finally tell that her slow month, which had produced ninety-eight bottles sold, had genuinely fallen short of break-even rather than simply feeling slow, and she adjusted her production plan for the following month accordingly. Ilda's two years without a break-even figure had not meant the business was doing badly. It had simply left her guessing either way, and only calculating the number ever gave her something concrete to measure a slow month against. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Running a business for months or years without ever calculating a break-even volume leaves an owner unable to distinguish a genuine loss from ordinary variation, exactly the position Ilda found herself in during her slow month. Treating the break-even number as a target to reach rather than a floor to clear can lead to satisfaction at a volume that leaves little or no actual profit. 2.7 Break-Even Answers One Question, Not Every Question Ilda's break-even figure told her precisely how many bottles covered her fixed costs each month. That figure alone did not tell her which flavours sold best or how to grow the business further, and treating it as the full picture rather than one useful measurement among several would have been its own kind of mistake. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to calculate the break-even volume a product or service needs before it turns a profit. Study Session 4 turns from knowing the minimum volume needed to comparing how profitable different products or services actually are once that volume is reached.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own business or a business you know. Has a break-even volume ever been calculated for it? 2. Calculate the break-even volume for one real product or service, separating fixed costs from the margin each unit earns. Practical Output: Practical Output A break-even calculation for one real product or service, showing fixed costs, margin per unit, and the resulting minimum sales volume. 7.0 References and Further Reading Sintha, L. (2020). Importance of break-even analysis for the micro, small and medium enterprises. International Journal of Research, GRANTHAALAYAH, 8(6), 212 to 218. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Judges 7:7, on being reduced to the exact three hundred men needed, no more. Qur'an, Surah Al-Anfal 8:66, on the burden being lightened, a steadfast hundred able to overcome two hundred.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Achol discovered several of her loaves sold for barely more than they cost once firewood, labour and rent were included. What did this reveal?
options: Achol's flour and sugar figures had been recorded inaccurately
Costing a product from materials alone, without labour or overhead, can leave a price sitting far closer to the true cost than it appears
Bread stalls in Yei should not sell bread at a fixed price
Achol had been overcharging her customers
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Working Out the True Cost of a Unit or Service) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Bigambo, Marandu and Elias's 2023 study of Dar es Salaam SMEs, what pattern did they find in how prices were set?
options: Most enterprises priced using a full cost including labour and overhead
Many enterprises set prices using only direct material cost, leaving out labour and overhead almost entirely
Enterprises never considered material cost when setting prices
Prices were set entirely by copying competitors
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Working Out the True Cost of a Unit or Service) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing with a shared cost such as rent or firewood?
options: Ignoring it entirely when working out a unit's cost
Spreading it evenly across the units typically produced in that period
Charging it only to the first unit made each day
Treating it as a one-time cost that never needs recalculating
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Working Out the True Cost of a Unit or Service) before continuing.

quiz.q: Hodan's most heavily embroidered dresses carried almost no margin, while simpler dresses carried a large one. What did this reveal?
options: Hodan's customers had been underpaying her deliberately
Pricing by instinct, without a deliberate margin, can leave the most demanding work priced far below what a consistent margin would suggest
Embroidery businesses should not sell detailed dresses
Hodan's true cost figures had been calculated incorrectly
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Setting a Margin on Top of True Cost) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Ndwandwe and Khoza's 2026 study of South African SMEs, what relationship was found?
options: No relationship between pricing strategy and business outcomes
A significant and positive relationship between deliberate pricing strategy and both growth and sustainability
A negative relationship between pricing strategy and growth
Pricing strategy only mattered for the largest enterprises surveyed
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Setting a Margin on Top of True Cost) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend deciding before pricing any individual item?
options: Nothing; each item should be priced purely on instinct
A margin, whether a percentage or a fixed amount, chosen in advance
The lowest price a competitor charges
Whichever price a customer suggests first
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Setting a Margin on Top of True Cost) before continuing.

modules.title: Part 2
modules.overview: Costing, Pricing and Profit Management — Part 2. Study each session, complete the reflection and practical output, and pass the part quiz before moving forward.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Comparing Profitability Across Products or Services

blocks.text: Introduction Mamello Ramaisa runs a small catering stall in Mokhotlong with several dishes on offer, and had always assumed her most popular, best-selling dish was also her most profitable one, until properly allocating costs across her whole menu revealed that a quieter, less popular dish actually earned a far higher margin, while the flagship dish barely covered its own true cost. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about analysing a product portfolio in the context of SMEs. Distinguish popularity from profitability. Apply a method for comparing contribution margin across products or services. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The Best-Seller That Barely Broke Even Mamello Ramaisa's catering stall in Mokhotlong offered several dishes, and one in particular sold more than any other, leading Mamello to assume for years that it was also her most profitable item. When Mamello finally sat down and allocated her full costs, ingredients, fuel, and a fair share of stall rent, across every dish on her menu rather than treating them as one shared pool, the best-selling dish turned out to earn only a slim margin, while a much quieter dish carried a contribution margin several times larger. 2.2 What Research Found About Analysing a Product Portfolio Gelmar Garcia-Vidal, Alexander Sanchez-Rodriguez, Reyner Perez-Campdesuner and Rodobaldo Martinez-Vivar proposed a contribution margin and quantity matrix for analysing product portfolios among SMEs in a 2023 paper, building on and critiquing the traditional BCG matrix used by larger firms. The proposed matrix allowed SMEs to classify their products by both contribution margin and sales quantity, revealing which items were quietly being carried by others rather than earning their own way. 2.3 Comparing Contribution Margin Across Offerings Allocating Costs to Each Product Rather Than One Shared Pool Working out the true cost of each individual product or service, rather than lumping all costs together as one general business expense, is the only way to see which specific items are actually carrying their own weight. Ranking Products by Margin, Not by Sales Volume Alone Listing products side by side by the margin each one earns, separately from how many units of each sell, surfaces the gap between what looks successful and what is actually profitable. 2.4 Key Practices Allocate costs to each individual product or service instead of lumping them into one shared total. Rank products or services by contribution margin, not by sales volume alone. Check whether a high-volume item is being quietly subsidised by others. Revisit the comparison whenever a recipe, process or cost changes noticeably. 2.5 A Worked Example: Mamello's Menu Comparison Mamello worked out the true cost of each of her five regular dishes and set the resulting margin for each one side by side, discovering that her best-selling stew carried a margin of only about eight maloti per plate, while a beef and vegetable dish she sold far less often carried a margin of nearly thirty maloti. She began gently steering undecided customers toward the higher-margin dish and adjusted the stew's price slightly upward to bring its own margin closer in line. Within a month, Mamello's overall profit had risen noticeably even though her total number of plates sold had barely changed, since a larger share of what she sold now carried a genuinely worthwhile margin. Mamello's assumption that her best-seller was also her best earner was an easy one for anyone to have made. Nobody had ever actually checked it against the true cost behind each dish, and only comparing margins directly ever showed which item was truly earning its place on the menu. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Assuming that a product's popularity reflects its profitability, without ever allocating costs to it individually, can leave a business's most celebrated item as one of its weakest earners, exactly what Mamello found with her stew. Comparing products only by how many units sell, rather than by the margin each one earns, hides exactly the gap a contribution margin comparison is meant to reveal. 2.7 Selling the Most Is Not the Same as Earning the Most Mamello's stew had genuinely been her top seller for years, drawing customers back again and again. A dish's popularity had never been a reliable stand-in for its earnings, and only allocating true cost to it individually ever showed how thin its margin actually was next to a much quieter item on the same menu. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to compare profitability across products or services using contribution margin rather than sales volume alone. Study Session 5 turns from comparing one product against another to understanding how a change in overall sales volume affects profit.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about the products or services you offer. Do you know which one earns the highest margin, or only which one sells the most? 2. Compare the contribution margin of at least three real products or services, ranking them from highest to lowest margin. Practical Output: Practical Output A contribution margin comparison across at least three real products or services, ranked from highest to lowest margin. 7.0 References and Further Reading Garcia-Vidal, G., Sanchez-Rodriguez, A., Perez-Campdesuner, R., & Martinez-Vivar, R. (2023). Contribution margin and quantity matrix to analyze the product portfolio in the context of SMEs. Cogent Business and Management, 10(1), 2233272. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Matthew 25:16, on trading five talents and making five more besides. Qur'an, Surah Al-Kahf 18:34, on one man boasting to his companion of greater wealth and more men.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Seeing How Volume Changes Affect Profit

blocks.text: Introduction Fatima Combo was widowed three years ago and has since run a small vanilla curing business alone from her home in Fomboni, and had assumed that a drop in sales would cost her roughly the same proportion in profit, until a month where sales fell by only a fifth left her profit down by nearly half, because her fixed costs, the curing shed's lease and a fixed transport contract, stayed exactly the same regardless of how much vanilla moved through them. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about cost volume profit analysis and managerial decisions. Distinguish a fixed cost from a variable cost. Apply a method for projecting how a change in sales volume affects profit. Recognise why profit does not move in a straight line with sales. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Fifth Less in Sales, Nearly Half Less in Profit Fatima Combo's vanilla curing business in Fomboni had, for most of its existence, seen profit rise and fall roughly alongside sales, which led Fatima to assume the relationship between the two was simple and proportional. During one month, sales fell by only about a fifth compared to the month before, yet profit fell by nearly half, a gap that made no sense to Fatima until she separated her costs into what stayed fixed regardless of volume, the curing shed's lease and a fixed transport contract, and what actually varied with how much vanilla she processed. 2.2 What Research Found About Cost Volume Profit Analysis Ahmed Mohamed surveyed 88 respondents working in accounting and finance departments of manufacturing firms in Mogadishu, Somalia, for a 2022 study on the role of cost volume profit analysis in managerial decision-making. A significant relationship was found between the split of fixed and variable costs and the quality of decisions managers were able to make, with firms that separated the two clearly able to anticipate the effect of a change in volume far more accurately than those that did not. 2.3 Projecting How Volume Affects Profit Separating What Stays Fixed From What Actually Varies Sorting every cost into one of two groups, those that stay the same no matter how much is produced and those that rise and fall with volume, is the first step to understanding why a change in sales does not translate into an equal change in profit. Projecting a Volume Change Against Both Cost Types Separately Working out how a rise or fall in sales affects variable costs proportionally, while fixed costs stay untouched, shows why profit can swing by a larger percentage than sales did in either direction. 2.4 Key Practices Sort every cost into fixed, which stays constant, or variable, which moves with volume. Project how a change in sales volume affects variable costs proportionally. Remember that fixed costs stay the same in total even as volume rises or falls. Use this split to anticipate a swing in profit before it happens, not only to explain it afterward. 2.5 A Worked Example: Fatima's Fixed and Variable Split Fatima worked out that her shed lease and transport contract together came to a fixed eighteen thousand francs a month regardless of how much vanilla passed through, while curing supplies and packaging varied directly with the quantity processed. When she modelled a further ten percent drop in sales against that split, the projection showed profit falling by close to twenty percent, a figure that matched what had actually happened the previous slow month almost exactly. With the projection in hand, Fatima began building a small buffer during stronger months specifically to absorb the sharper swings a slow month now caused in profit, rather than being caught off guard by them again. Fatima's earlier assumption that profit and sales moved together proportionally was a perfectly natural place to start. That assumption had simply never accounted for costs that refused to move regardless of volume, and only separating fixed from variable costs ever explained why a modest drop in sales had hit her profit so much harder. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Assuming that profit moves in the same proportion as sales, without separating fixed costs from variable ones, makes it impossible to anticipate how sharply a slow period will actually cut into profit, exactly what caught Fatima off guard. Treating all costs as though they vary with volume hides the specific role fixed costs play in amplifying a swing in either direction. 2.7 A Small Change in Sales Can Be a Large Change in Profit Fatima's sales had fallen by only a modest fifth during that difficult month. That modest fall had never been a reliable guide to how much profit would fall alongside it, and only separating fixed costs from variable ones ever showed why the two figures had moved so differently from each other. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to separate fixed from variable costs and project how a change in volume actually affects profit. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how cost and margin assumptions are reviewed and kept current rather than left to quietly go stale.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own costs. Which ones would stay exactly the same next month even if your sales dropped sharply? 2. Separate one real month of costs into fixed and variable, then project how a ten percent change in sales would affect profit. Practical Output: Practical Output A fixed and variable cost split for one real month, with a projection showing how a ten percent change in sales volume would affect profit. 7.0 References and Further Reading Mohamed, A. (2022). The role of cost volume profit analysis on the managerial decision-making in manufacturing firms in Mogadishu, Somalia. Zenodo. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 14:4, on there being no increase without the strength of an ox, though the crib stays clean without one. Qur'an, Surah Al-An'am 6:141, on eating from the fruit when it ripens and paying its due on the day of harvest.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Reviewing and Updating Cost and Margin Assumptions Over Time

blocks.text: Introduction Mahamat Youssouf runs a small metalworking shop in Abeche, and had set his prices and cost figures once, years earlier, and never revisited them even as the price of steel and fuel climbed substantially over time, until a rough month forced him to recalculate his true costs from scratch and discover how far his margins had quietly eroded from what he still believed them to be. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about how often firms actually review and change their prices. Distinguish a cost assumption that has been recently reviewed from one that has gone stale. Apply a method for periodically reviewing and updating cost and margin assumptions. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Prices That Had Not Moved in Years Mahamat Youssouf's metalworking shop in Abeche had used the same cost figures and prices for several years, set once when the business began and never deliberately revisited since. Over that time, the price of steel and fuel had climbed considerably, but Mahamat's prices had stayed almost exactly where they started. A rough month with unusually thin cash reserves finally pushed Mahamat to recalculate his true costs from the ground up, revealing margins that had eroded far more than he had realised, in some cases to almost nothing. 2.2 What Research Found About How Often Firms Review Their Prices Alan Blinder and colleagues interviewed two hundred corporate price setters across a national, multi-industry sample for a study published in 1998, examining how often firms actually reviewed and changed their prices in practice. The median firm was found to change its prices only about once a year, a far lower frequency than many of the firms themselves assumed, and a substantial share of firms reported implicit habits that kept prices stable well beyond what changing costs alone would justify. 2.3 Reviewing and Updating Cost and Margin Assumptions Setting a Fixed Point to Review Cost Figures Choosing a specific point, whether every quarter or every time a major input's price shifts noticeably, to recalculate true cost and margin keeps those figures from drifting unnoticed for years at a time. Comparing Current Costs Against the Original Assumptions Directly Placing the figures a price was originally built on side by side with the actual current cost of the same inputs makes any gap between the two immediately visible, rather than something that only surfaces during a genuine crisis. 2.4 Key Practices Set a fixed point, such as every quarter, to review cost and margin figures. Recalculate immediately whenever a major input's price shifts noticeably. Compare current input costs directly against the figures a price was originally built on. Treat a long-unreviewed price as a risk to check, not a settled fact to trust. 2.5 A Worked Example: Mahamat's Quarterly Cost Review After his rough month, Mahamat set a fixed point every three months to pull current steel and fuel prices and compare them directly against the figures his prices had originally been built on, adjusting his prices whenever the gap grew large enough to matter. The first review alone showed that steel had risen by close to a third since his prices were last set, and Mahamat adjusted his prices accordingly rather than waiting for another rough month to force the issue. A year into the new habit, Mahamat's margins had stayed consistently close to what he intended them to be, with no single quarter producing the kind of shock his original years of unreviewed prices had built up unnoticed. Mahamat's original prices had not been wrong on the day he set them. They had simply been left in place long after the costs behind them had moved on, and only a fixed habit of reviewing them ever kept that gap from growing large enough to threaten the business again. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Setting prices once and never deliberately revisiting them allows rising input costs to erode a margin quietly over years, exactly what happened to Mahamat's metalworking shop. Waiting for a crisis, such as a rough month with thin cash reserves, to trigger a cost review rather than reviewing on a fixed schedule means the erosion is often severe by the time it is finally caught. 2.7 A Price Set Correctly Once Does Not Stay Correct Forever Mahamat's original prices had genuinely reflected his true costs on the day he calculated them. Being correct at that starting point had never guaranteed they would remain correct years later, and only a deliberate habit of reviewing cost figures against current reality ever caught how far they had drifted. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to review and update cost and margin assumptions on a fixed schedule rather than leaving them to go stale. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Inventory and Stock Record Keeping, the next course in Pathway 57.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own prices. When were they last checked against the actual current cost of what goes into them? 2. Compare the current cost of your main inputs against the figures your prices were originally built on, and adjust at least one price if a meaningful gap exists. Practical Output: Practical Output A cost review comparing current input prices against the original figures a real price was built on, with at least one price adjusted if a meaningful gap is found. 7.0 References and Further Reading Blinder, A.S., Canetti, E.R.D., Lebow, D.E., & Rudd, J.B. (1998). Asking about prices: A new approach to understanding price stickiness. Russell Sage Foundation. quiz.q: Mamello's best-selling dish carried a far thinner margin than a much quieter dish on her menu. What did this reveal?
options: Mamello's ingredients had been priced incorrectly
A product's popularity does not necessarily reflect how profitable it actually is once true cost is allocated to it individually
Catering stalls should only sell one dish at a time
Mamello's customers preferred cheaper dishes
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Comparing Profitability Across Products or Services) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Garcia-Vidal and colleagues' 2023 study, what did their proposed contribution margin and quantity matrix reveal for SMEs?
options: That every product in a portfolio earns roughly the same margin
Which items were quietly being carried by others rather than earning their own way
That sales volume is always the best measure of profitability
That SMEs should not analyse their product portfolios at all
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Comparing Profitability Across Products or Services) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing instead of treating all costs as one shared pool?
options: Ignoring costs entirely when comparing products
Allocating costs to each individual product or service
Assuming every product shares an identical cost
Comparing products only by their selling price
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Comparing Profitability Across Products or Services) before continuing.

quiz.q: Fatima's sales fell by a fifth, but her profit fell by nearly half. What did this reveal?
options: Fatima's vanilla curing process had failed that month
Fixed costs that stay the same regardless of volume can cause profit to swing by a larger proportion than sales did
Vanilla businesses in Fomboni should not track monthly sales
Fatima had been overcharging her customers
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Seeing How Volume Changes Affect Profit) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Mohamed's 2022 study of Mogadishu manufacturing firms, what was found about separating fixed and variable costs?
options: It had no effect on the quality of managerial decisions
Firms that separated the two clearly could anticipate the effect of a volume change far more accurately
Only large firms benefited from separating fixed and variable costs
Variable costs had no relationship to managerial decision-making
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Seeing How Volume Changes Affect Profit) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing with every cost a business carries?
options: Treating every cost as though it varies with volume
Sorting each cost into fixed, which stays constant, or variable, which moves with volume
Ignoring costs that seem small in any given month
Assuming all costs behave identically
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Seeing How Volume Changes Affect Profit) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Achol discovered several of her loaves sold for barely more than they cost once firewood, labour and rent were included. What did this reveal?
options: Achol's flour and sugar figures had been recorded inaccurately
Costing a product from materials alone, without labour or overhead, can leave a price sitting far closer to the true cost than it appears
Bread stalls in Yei should not sell bread at a fixed price
Achol had been overcharging her customers
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Working Out the True Cost of a Unit or Service) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Bigambo, Marandu and Elias's 2023 study of Dar es Salaam SMEs, what pattern did they find in how prices were set?
options: Most enterprises priced using a full cost including labour and overhead
Many enterprises set prices using only direct material cost, leaving out labour and overhead almost entirely
Enterprises never considered material cost when setting prices
Prices were set entirely by copying competitors
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Working Out the True Cost of a Unit or Service) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend doing with a shared cost such as rent or firewood?
options: Ignoring it entirely when working out a unit's cost
Spreading it evenly across the units typically produced in that period
Charging it only to the first unit made each day
Treating it as a one-time cost that never needs recalculating
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Working Out the True Cost of a Unit or Service) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Hodan's most heavily embroidered dresses carried almost no margin, while simpler dresses carried a large one. What did this reveal?
options: Hodan's customers had been underpaying her deliberately
Pricing by instinct, without a deliberate margin, can leave the most demanding work priced far below what a consistent margin would suggest
Embroidery businesses should not sell detailed dresses
Hodan's true cost figures had been calculated incorrectly
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Setting a Margin on Top of True Cost) before continuing.

A negative relationship between pricing strategy and growth
Pricing strategy only mattered for the largest enterprises surveyed

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend deciding before pricing any individual item?
options: Nothing; each item should be priced purely on instinct
A margin, whether a percentage or a fixed amount, chosen in advance
The lowest price a competitor charges
Whichever price a customer suggests first

Fruit juice businesses in Assomada should not track monthly sales
